sm: Douglas Axe introduces what he calls functional coherence, meaning the hierarchical arrangement of parts that each contribute in a coordinated way to a high-level function. He points to a violin, a mechanical watch and a smartphone as familiar inventions, then zooms through the human body, the eye, the retina's rod and cone cells, a generic animal cell, and finally the ribosome. He argues that living things show the same structure, so our intuition of design is supported by observation, scientific questions and deductions. He says a common sense argument, rather than a technical one, most clearly undermines the Darwinian worldview, and that his book explains this with pictures for non-scientists.

Axe says that when critics raise objections like fossils, DNA, horizontal gene transfer, co-option or the molecular clock, people can bring the discussion back to intuition. On natural selection, he says it is an accidental cause with no purpose or intent, so it cannot do the work of knowhow. He quotes Richard Dawkins's first chapter, which says there are vastly more ways of being dead than alive, and that random assembly of cells would never produce something that works. Axe argues that Dawkins thinks calling natural selection non-random solves this problem. In his view, selection only acts once something already works to keep itself alive, so it cannot solve the improbability hurdle Dawkins acknowledges.
